content: The human T-lymphotropic viruses, type I (HTLV-I) and type II (HTLV-II), are retroviruses that infect humans. They are distinct from the human immunodeficiency viruses (HIV-1 and HIV-2), which cause acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). HTLV-I and HTLV-II belong to the oncovirus subfamily of retroviruses and are capable of transforming human lymphocytes into self-sustaining cells in vitro. These viruses are only distantly related to HIV, which belongs to the lentivirus subfamily. HTLV-I and HTLV-II infections are primarily detected through serological testing. The presence of antibodies to HTLV-I or HTLV-II in a person’s blood indicates infection. Since 1988, all blood donations in the United States have been screened for HTLV-I antibodies. However, the licensed screening tests, which use HTLV-I antigens, do not reliably differentiate between HTLV-I and HTLV-II antibodies. Additionally, these tests vary in their sensitivity to detect HTLV-II antibodies. Confirmatory tests, such as Western immunoblot and radioimmunoprecipitation assays, are used to verify seroreactivity, but they also cannot reliably distinguish between the two viruses. In the first year of HTLV-I/II blood screening in the United States, approximately 2,000 infected blood donors were identified. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing revealed that about half of these individuals were infected with HTLV-I and the other half with HTLV-II. Infected donors are counseled and permanently deferred from donating blood. However, because PCR testing is not routinely available, many individuals with serological reactivity are informed that they are infected with HTLV-I/II without specific identification of the virus. This uncertainty complicates counseling due to the differing epidemiological and clinical implications of HTLV-I and HTLV-II infections. Until recently, the only reliable method to differentiate HTLV-I from HTLV-II was through PCR. However, investigational peptideand recombinant protein-based serological assays have been developed to more easily distinguish between antibodies to HTLV-I and HTLV-II. Preliminary data suggest these tests are potentially useful for typing serum samples. These investigational tests are not yet widely available, and their use is primarily limited to research settings. HTLV-I infection is endemic in southwestern Japan, the Caribbean basin, Melanesia, and parts of Africa. In some endemic areas, prevalence rates as high as 15% have been reported in the general population. Seroprevalence increases with age and is typically higher among women in older age groups. In the United States, approximately half of HTLV-I/II-seropositive blood donors are infected with HTLV-I. Most HTLV-I-infected donors report a history of birth in endemic countries or sexual contact with individuals from the Caribbean or Japan. Smaller percentages report injecting drug use or blood transfusion as risk factors. HTLV-I is transmitted through mother-to-child transmission (primarily via breastfeeding), sexual contact, blood transfusion, and sharing contaminated needles. Approximately 25% of breastfed infants born to HTLV-I-seropositive mothers acquire the infection. Intrauterine or perinatal transmission occurs less frequently, with about 5% of children born to infected mothers but not breastfed acquiring the infection. Sexual transmission is more efficient from males to females than vice versa. Transmission through blood transfusion occurs with cellular blood products but not with plasma or plasma derivatives. The probability of transmission decreases with longer storage durations of blood products, likely due to the depletion of infected T-lymphocytes. HTLV-I is not transmitted through casual contact. Healthcare workers caring for HTLV-I-infected individuals need only be concerned about percutaneous exposure to contaminated blood. Universal precautions are sufficient to prevent transmission in healthcare settings. Two diseases are definitively associated with HTLV-I: adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL) and HTLV-I-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP). ATL is a malignancy of HTLV-I-infected CD4+ T-lymphocytes, characterized by infiltration of lymph nodes, viscera, and skin with malignant cells. Circulating abnormal lymphocytes, known as flower cells, are typically observed. Median survival is 11 months from diagnosis, and conventional chemotherapy is not curative. HAM/TSP is a chronic, progressive neurologic disease characterized by spastic paraparesis, lower limb weakness, sensory disturbances, and urinary incontinence. Antibodies to HTLV-I are typically found in the cerebrospinal fluid of affected individuals. HTLV-II infection has not been clearly associated with any specific diseases. The virus is prevalent among injecting drug users in the United States and Europe and appears to be endemic in certain American Indian populations. HTLV-II is presumed to be transmitted similarly to HTLV-I, but less is known about its specific modes and efficiency of transmission. Serological testing for HTLV-I and HTLV-II involves screening serum specimens for antibodies using enzyme immunoassays. Confirmatory tests, such as Western immunoblot and radioimmunoprecipitation assays, are used to interpret reactive specimens. However, these tests cannot differentiate between HTLV-I and HTLV-II antibodies. Recent advances include the development of recombinant protein-based assays that may improve specificity in differentiating the two viruses. Blood donors who test seropositive for HTLV-I/II are notified and permanently deferred from donating blood. Counseling recommendations for HTLV-seropositive individuals include advising them to refrain from donating blood, sharing needles, or breastfeeding. They should also consider using barrier precautions to prevent sexual transmission. Periodic medical evaluations by knowledgeable physicians are recommended for HTLV-infected individuals.
